transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-26
Time: 15:00 UTC (52 minutes)
Attendees: Maya Ortiz (Redwood AE), Jonah Park (Redwood SE), Alex Chen (CTO - Solstice), Priya Kapoor (Lead ML Engineer), Marcus Lee (Head of Security)
---
Auto-summary (auto-gen): Walkthrough of JSON mode and tool calling, emphasis on safety and auditability for payments use-case. Next steps pinned to pilot and security docs.
---
00:00:00 Maya Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood, I'm the AE, with Jonah our SE. Quick intros?
00:00:12 Alex Chen: Hi Alex here, CTO at Solstice. We run payment reconciliation and fraud analytics, looking to reduce manual ops and speed up resolution.
00:00:20 Priya Kapoor: Priya, lead on ML infra. We're particularly focused on consistent output, schema enforcement, and latency SLA.
00:00:27 Marcus Lee: Marcus, security. We'll need encryption at rest, KMS, audit logs, and SSO integration.
00:00:35 Maya Ortiz: Great, high level agenda: JSON mode and schemas, function/tool calling patterns for your backend ops, console/Optimize recommendations, then Q&A and next steps. Jonah will drive the demo.
00:00:48 Jonah Park: Cool, I'm gonna share screen — starting with the console. Note: our demo data is synthetic, obviously. First bit is typed responses: we show a schema contract for a reconciliation action output.
00:01:10 Jonah Park: (screen) Here's a simple JSON schema: fields for transaction_id, match_status enum, suggested_action object with reason and confidence. We enforce the schema at runtime and can return machine-parseable actions that you can wire into your orchestration.
00:01:34 Priya Kapoor: Quick q — if the model hallucinate a field or types don't match, how strict is the enforcement? Do you fail the call or return a sanitized fallback?
00:01:44 Jonah Park: Good question. We have a few modes — strict mode returns an error if the response violates the schema so you can route to a human; resilient mode attempts to coerce or fill missing fields and logs the deviation. You can also provide a fallback policy — like call a lower-cost model or a deterministic rule-based function.
00:02:05 Alex Chen: That fallback sounds useful. For payments we can't have silent wrong actions.
00:02:11 Jonah Park: Exactly. Also show we have action-contracts: if the model suggests "release_funds" we require an additional sign-off field and a policy check before the tool executes.
00:02:28 Marcus Lee: What about authorization on tool calls? We don't want the model calling our payout API without RBAC checks.
00:02:35 Jonah Park: We recommend a proxy pattern — Redwood issues a typed action, then your backend verifies RBAC, checks audit policy, and invokes the actual payout. The console also shows a trace: who generated the action, which model and prompt used, token counts, and an immutable audit event.
00:02:55 Marcus Lee: Nice. On encryption — KMS and HSM support? Key rotation?
00:03:02 Maya Ortiz: We support KMS integration and customer-managed keys in Private mode. For Hosted we use AES with rotation and can offer bring-your-own-key via our KMS bridge for Dedicated/Private. We'll share the security whitepaper.
00:03:15 Alex Chen: Timing — can we run dedicated in our VPC? We need isolation for PCI scope.
00:03:22 Jonah Park: Yes, Redwood Private supports V P C deployments and on-prem package if needed. Dedicated capacity gives predictable throughput too. We'll map that in the pilot scope.
00:03:34 Jonah Park: Back to JSON mode — showing a live run: prompt: "Match TXN 4a9... to ledger entries and suggest action". Model returns structured JSON with match_status: "partial_match", suggested_action: {type: "hold", reason: "amount mismatch", confidence: 0.87}.
00:03:58 Priya Kapoor: Latency on that call?
00:04:02 Jonah Park: This run is on our hosted cluster; p95 is around 120ms for similar sized requests but that depends on token lengths, batching, and model variant. For lower latency we can choose a smaller quantized variant or configure routing to a low-latency pool.
00:04:18 Priya Kapoor: We need sub-150ms p95 for some interactive tools. Also throughput for batch reconciliation at night.
00:04:25 Jonah Park: Optimize covers that — we show queuing/batching dashboards and recommend batching windows for background jobs vs strict no-batch routes for interactive. We also give quantization profiles per model to balance cost/latency.
00:04:40 Alex Chen: If we do a pilot, what data flows into Redwood? We need to ensure PII never leaves our VPC for certain flows.
00:04:48 Maya Ortiz: You can set route policies: sensitive flows go to Private/Dedicated, while anonymized or low-risk requests go to Hosted. Token-level logging can be disabled for Private, and audit logging still works with local retention.
00:05:02 Marcus Lee: How auditable are the model decisions? We need immutable logs for every action suggested by the model, including the schema validation result and any fallback used.
00:05:10 Jonah Park: Console traces include the raw model output, validation result, and any transform applied. Those traces are stored as immutable events with cryptographic checksums in Dedicated/Private modes; we can also ship them to your SIEM.
00:05:25 Priya Kapoor: Can we do function calling that invokes internal microservices? For example: call /recon/match with structured payload?
00:05:33 Jonah Park: Yes — functions/tool-calling supports typed payloads. You can register a tool surface that accepts the schema we enforce. Tools run in a sandboxed environment if you enable our action sandbox so arbitrary code is restricted.
00:05:48 Alex Chen: Sandbox — does it run in our tenant? We prefer to keep the execution in our VPC for PII safety.
00:05:55 Jonah Park: For Private/Dedicated we can host the action runtime in your VPC. For Hosted we offer a restricted sandbox with strict egress rules and an allow-list for outbound endpoints.
00:06:08 Maya Ortiz: Jumping to safety guards — we showed a policy language that you can author for allowed actions, thresholds, and which roles can approve certain action types.
00:06:20 Marcus Lee: Is that policy versioned and auditable?
00:06:23 Jonah Park: Yes, policies are versioned and you can attach them to rollout groups. Changes are auditable with a who/when record.
00:06:31 Priya Kapoor: During the demo the typed response validator flagged a field mismatch — can you show that flow?
00:06:36 Jonah Park: Sure. (screen) The validator shows mismatch: expected number, got string for confidence. In strict mode the call failed and an event was raised to the human-in-the-loop queue. In resilient mode it coerced to numeric and added a "coercion" flag.
00:06:55 Priya Kapoor: Ok makes sense. For our pipelines, we prefer failure with explicit human review for any money-moving action.
00:07:03 Jonah Park: That's exactly a canary policy we recommend; we can automatically route failover to a manual approval queue in your dashboard.
00:07:11 Alex Chen: On costs — curious about per-token pricing vs fixed capacity. We have heavy nightly jobs — bulk reconciliation — and interactive case resolution during day.
00:07:21 Maya Ortiz: We typically do hybrid: Hosted per-token for exploratory and low-velocity flows; Dedicated reserved capacity for peak batch jobs; Optimize gives suggestions to quantize and batch night jobs to reduce unit cost. For your pilot we can propose a blended model.
00:07:36 Alex Chen: Competitors — we've eval'd Anthropic and OpenAI; any differentiation here?
00:07:41 Maya Ortiz: Customers tell us Redwood's differentiation is production-first tooling — the typed output enforcement, builtin rollback and ambient guardrails, and unified experience across Private/Dedicated/Hosted. We also provide deeper observability for cost per token and per-route tracing.
00:07:55 Marcus Lee: Any SOC2 / ISO certs we can reference?
00:07:59 Maya Ortiz: Yes, SOC 2 Type II — we'll attach the report, and we have ISO documentation too. We'll send those to Marcus.
00:08:07 Priya Kapoor: Demo question — can the console simulate schema regressions and run a suite of test prompts for regression alerts?
00:08:15 Jonah Park: Yes, Evals integration: you can attach a prompt set to a model version and we run continuous evaluation. If schema drift or quality regression occurs, it triggers alerts and you can pin a rollback.
00:08:29 Alex Chen: Good. Any concerns about hallucination of payout instructions?
00:08:34 Jonah Park: That's precisely why we recommend typed actions + backend verification. The model suggests, your system enforces and only then executes. Also policy checks and manual signoff for money-moving ops.
00:08:47 Priya Kapoor: About the trial org — can you provision a sandbox tenant with Dedicated-ish settings so we can run latency tests?
00:08:54 Maya Ortiz: We can provision a pilot org that mirrors dedicated routing and gives you control over logging and KMS stubs. It won't be full Dedicated hardware but we can simulate the latency/throughput patterns and run benchmarks.
00:09:05 Alex Chen: That's acceptable for initial validation.
00:09:09 Jonah Park: Quick note: Optimize suggested changing batch window from 500ms to 2s for night jobs and applying int8 quantization for that model to cut token cost ~45% while keeping latency slack.
00:09:23 Priya Kapoor: Would like to see those numbers on our actual workload.
00:09:26 Jonah Park: We will run a benchmark with your prompt set during the pilot.
00:09:31 Maya Ortiz: Jumping to risks — any compliance blockers you foresee?
00:09:35 Marcus Lee: We need data residency for EU customers and proof-of-concept for KMS integration. Also SAML SSO and RBAC.
00:09:43 Maya Ortiz: Noted. Redwood supports SAML/SSO, role-based teams in the console, and Private deployments give data residency controls. We'll include KMS integration checklist.
00:09:55 Alex Chen: Pricing — rough order of magnitude for 30-day pilot with dedicated-ish sandbox and bench session?
00:10:02 Maya Ortiz: We'll send a pilot pricing sheet — generally pilots are capped and we can include a performance bench block in the scope.
00:10:10 Priya Kapoor: One more technical: how do you handle KV cache when you do tool-calling with long histories? We have long context for recon conversations.
00:10:18 Jonah Park: Our runtime supports KV caching and dynamic eviction policies. For tool calls we snapshot relevant keys into the request; you can also pin persistent KV per-tenant for session wiring. There are protections to avoid leaking unrelated tenant data.
00:10:33 Priya Kapoor: Good.
00:10:36 Maya Ortiz: We'll wrap up with a quick recap and next steps. Jonah, can you summarize the technical ask?
00:10:41 Jonah Park: Sure. Tech ask: run a pilot with typed schema-driven actions for payment reconciliation, include a performance benchmark, set strict validation for all money-moving actions, enable KMS stub in pilot, and provide console access for lineage/audit review.
00:11:00 Alex Chen: That matches our expectations. Timeline: aim to start pilot first week of Sept.
00:11:05 Maya Ortiz: Perfect. We'll send the pilot proposal by Sept 1 and demo recording + sample schemas by Aug 28. Any final Qs?
00:11:14 Marcus Lee: Please include SOC2 and KMS docs in the materials. Also list of supported key providers.
00:11:21 Maya Ortiz: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow-up with the artifacts and schedule.
00:11:27 Alex Chen: Thanks all.
